fetched_contents.text: 12.0 Identification and Tracking Systems State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology Chapter Contents * Chapter Glossary * 12.1 Introduction * 12.2 Identification and Tracking Ground Systems * 12.3 Tracking Aids * 12.4 Devices that Communicate Position and ID via Radio * 12.5 Devices that Use Coded Light Signals * 12.5.1 Van Atta Arrays and RF Interrogation Receivers * 12.5.2 Laser-Interrogated Corner Cube Reflectors * 12.5.3 Passive Increase in Albedo * 12.6 Future Efforts * 12.7 Summary * References Chapter Glossary 12.1 Introduction In the past, most launches involved a single, large satellite launching on a dedicated launch vehicle. Small satellites as secondary payloads were sometimes “dropped off” along the way to the primary payload’s orbit or rode along to the final orbit with the primary payload. In either case, it typically was not that difficult for tracking radars to distinguish between primary and secondary payloads based on size and operational parameters. Recently, however, multi-manifest or “rideshare” launches have become more common, and providers (1)(2)(3) are launching multiple CubeSats, or bundling CubeSats and other smaller payloads with larger payloads to fill up the excess capacity of almost any given launch vehicle. For technical and cost reasons, such launches generally deploy small satellites and CubeSats into very similar orbits over a short time window. “Batch” launches with a lack of separation between satellites can prevent effective tracking and create “CubeSat confusion” (4). When CubeSats are deployed close together in space and time, they can be difficult to distinguish from each other by tracking radars, making it difficult to determine which orbits correlate to which spacecraft, preventing a unique orbital state for each object from being added to the catalog of on-orbit objects (5)(6). Even when successful, these objects frequently remain unidentified for a lengthy period of time. It is not unusual for the process to take weeks to months to sort out which object is which, while some may never be positively identified at all. If the orbital states cannot be determined and the spacecraft cannot be added to the catalog of on-orbit objects, neighboring satellites may be unaware of close approaches, thereby hindering their ability to mitigate risks of collision. Furthermore, if identification is not resolved then conjunction warnings may not be sent to the responsible party or – even worse – they may be erroneously sent to an incorrect party if a mis-identification occurs. Due to their standardized shape and size, CubeSats look very similar to one another, especially when they are in orbit hundreds of kilometers away. If there are unidentified objects from a launch, then the possible number of associations of object identifications (IDs) to tracked objects scales as n! (n-factorial, where n is the number of unidentified space objects from the launch). For example, if there are just two objects, say a payload and an upper stage, there are two ways in which you can associate the IDs with the tracked objects, and even that can be a challenge (7). However, if there are ten unidentified objects, there are 3,628,800 possible combinations; with 20 this rises to 2.4×1018 combinations. The magnitude of the problem becomes large very quickly. Annually, several multi-manifest deployments already deliver over 100+ objects per launch. As new launch vehicles come to market, this capacity is anticipated to increase to several hundred objects per launch, meaning that an already acute problem will only intensify. Small satellites can improve their chances of being identified and tracked through good coordination with tracking agencies pre-launch, through community sharing of position/velocity, maneuvering, and covariance data in clearly defined, consistent, standardized formats (ex: Orbit Comprehensive Message (OCM)), and through careful selection of deployment direction and timing (8). Good spacecraft design choices can also improve the chances of small satellites surviving launch and early orbit (9), and can even make use of in-space commercial radio networks as a “back-up” method of communicating, should primary systems fail (10). However, despite improvements in both design and coordination, many small satellites still go unidentified. This has led to the introduction of tracking aids – independent systems that help owners and trackers identify small satellites and CubeSats, in some cases even if the satellite is malfunctioning. Even if a small satellite is trackable (or rendered trackable through one of the enhancements discussed below), it is important that this position information be combined with satellite planned maneuver information and packaged into a predicted ephemeris that can be sent regularly (at least daily) to a conjunction assessment (CA) screening authority. The only way that CA screenings can be meaningful is if a satellite’s future position is used by the screening authority in the screening process. Non-cooperative tracking, even if it is well and frequently performed, cannot anticipate satellite maneuvers, and this information is essential to a robust conjunction assessment system. Maneuverable satellites (which include satellites that employ non-propulsive trajectory modification methods, such as differential drag) must assemble and furnish durable predicted ephemerides to the screening authority, either through indigenous means (i.e., unaided tracking and their own flight dynamics system’s production of a predicted ephemeris) or via one of the position determination approaches to be described in order to ensure the operators are aware of close approaches with them. fetched_contents.text: Cislunar initial orbit determination for angles-only short arcs based on multi-constrained optimization Highlights * • This paper presents and assesses a multi-constrained optimization algorithm for IOD in cislunar space using angles-only short-arc observations. * • By integrating measurement, dynamic, and inherent orbital constraints, this approach is designed to enhance the convergence success rate and accuracy of cislunar IOD. * • The algorithm’s performance was validated by setting up multiple simulation scenarios under a high-fidelity ephemeris model. * • Numerical simulations demonstrate that, compared to three other cislunar IOD algorithms, our algorithm exhibits stronger robustness under varying observation geometries, a higher convergence success rate, and improved accuracy. Abstract Under lunar gravity, spacecraft orbits in cislunar space are non-Keplerian, rendering traditional two-body-based initial orbit determination (IOD) methods ineffective. Moreover, their lengthy orbital periods mean even hours of observation capture only a tiny fraction of the orbit, making cislunar IOD a challenging short-arc problem. This paper presents and assesses a multi-constrained optimization algorithm for IOD in cislunar space using angles-only short-arc observations. By integrating measurement, dynamic, and inherent orbital constraints, this approach is designed to enhance the convergence success rate and accuracy of cislunar IOD. Numerical simulations demonstrate that, compared to three other cislunar IOD algorithms, the algorithm presented herein exhibits stronger robustness under varying observation geometries, a higher convergence success rate, and improved accuracy. Introduction Cislunar space, the region encompassing the Earth-Moon system, is a critical domain for space exploration and operational activities. Effective space situational awareness (SSA) in this domain is essential for various applications, including the space traffic management and the scientific researches [1]. Optical sensors are widely applied to the SSA in the cislunar space, because they can accomplish a passive surveillance for nearly the whole cislunar space [2]. Optical sensors can only provide the angle-only measurements. When the angle-only measurements are available, the famous initial orbit determination (IOD) methods, such as the Laplace, Gauss, Double-R, and Gooding algorithms, have been widely applied to determine the initial orbits of spacecraft in the near Earth space [3,4]. However, these methods all assume the orbit of spacecraft is only affected by the gravity of Earth. For spacecraft orbiting in the cislunar space, the gravity of Moon cannot be neglected. In this case, the aforementioned methods will fail [5]. The problem of IOD in the cislunar space has been the subject of considerable research in recent literature. Existing initial orbit determination algorithms for cislunar space can be divided into several major categories. One category is admissible region-based cislunar IOD methods. The admissible region method was originally used to address the two-body IOD problem, determining an initial guess of the state by assuming the target satisfies certain physical assumptions. Hou et al. [6] constructed an admissible region for the cislunar IOD problem by employing the criterion of negative two-body energy, although this criterion is not universally valid in the three-body dynamical environment. Replacing hard constraints with a probabilistic representation (probability density functions of semi-major axis and eccentricity), Hussein et al. [7] proposed the probabilistic admissible region. However, in the three-body dynamical environment, the state of a spacecraft cannot be described by the six classical orbital elements, making it difficult to identify complementary variables analogous to the semi-major axis or eccentricity in two-body orbits, let alone their probability density functions. Bolden et al. [8] extended the probabilistic admissible region method to the cislunar IOD problem by leveraging the apparent magnitude of the target to estimate its slant range. However, the apparent magnitude depends on variables such as target radius, albedo, sun–target–observer angle, and sensor sensitivity. These details are seldom available as prior knowledge and particularly challenging to acquire for non-cooperative targets. Liu et al. [9] employed constraints including the ranges of Jacobi constants and geocentric two-body energies of periodic orbit families to construct an admissible region. In conjunction with Differential Algebra, they further proposed the CR3BP-DAIOD algorithm. Another category is optimization-based cislunar IOD methods. Smego et al. [10] proposed a two-stage cislunar IOD algorithm based on dynamic triangulation and nonlinear least squares estimation. This approach approximates an object’s motion as rectilinear over a short orbital segment, enabling dynamic triangulation to generate an initial full-state estimate. Heidrich et al. [11] presented a cislunar IOD algorithm based on sparse grid collocation, which substitutes traditional explicit numerical integration with implicit transcription. This approach formulates the problem as a large-scale sparse nonlinear programming problem (NLP), thereby requiring the use of efficient NLP solvers. Wu et al. [12] proposed a state transition tensors (STTs)-enhanced cislunar IOD method, which employs a forward-backward shooting technique to construct a state correction model. Jo et al. [13] proposed a cislunar IOD algorithm utilizing differential corrections. A key advantage of this method is its ease of implementation, as it relies solely on a simple iterative process. How to fuse and process heterogeneous data for improved tracking

The evidence points to a clear best practice: SSA data fusion should combine multiple sources into a single coherent picture of space objects, with a special emphasis on telemetry, tracking, and other SSA-relevant inputs. The NASA “Identification and Tracking Systems” source explains that SSA data is used to predict conjunctions and warn operators of dangerous close approaches, which implies that telemetry and tracking data are foundational inputs to the SSA system [N2-F2]. The Mobility Engineering Technology article explicitly states that the system fuses data from satellite telemetry, space weather, orbital proximity, and radio frequency input [N2-R2]. Ansys’s definition of SSA as the practice of characterizing, tracking, and predicting objects in space around Earth also supports the idea that tracking data are part of the core SSA workflow [N2-R4].

Best practices for fusing telemetry, tracking, and other data sources therefore include using a broad set of inputs, not relying on a single sensor type, and ensuring that the resulting data can support conjunction assessment and collision avoidance. The NASA source also highlights that good spacecraft coordination and standardized data formats such as Orbit Comprehensive Message (OCM) improve identification and tracking, which means that interoperability and standardized telemetry exchange are important fusion best practices [N2-F2]. In short, the evidence supports a multi-source, standardized, and interoperable fusion approach rather than a single-sensor-only strategy [N2-R2][N2-F2].

The role of data quality assessment and outlier handling is also implied by the evidence. The NASA source stresses that identification and tracking are difficult when objects are deployed closely together, leading to “CubeSat confusion” and a large number of possible identification combinations [N2-F2]. This suggests that raw observations are not enough: they need validation against known spacecraft characteristics, maneuver information, and covariance data. The same source also emphasizes that position information must be combined with planned maneuver information and packaged into a predicted ephemeris, because non-cooperative tracking alone cannot anticipate maneuvers and therefore cannot support robust conjunction assessment [N2-F2]. This is a key quality-assessment step: any measurement should be checked against expected maneuver behavior, and outliers or inconsistent observations should be flagged or excluded before they affect the ephemeris.

For outlier handling, the evidence indirectly supports rejection or downweighting of inconsistent or low-quality observations. The NASA source says that unidentified objects can remain unidentified for weeks or months, and that misidentification can lead to erroneous warnings being sent to the wrong party [N2-F2]. That implies that the fusion pipeline should include mechanisms to detect and resolve ambiguous associations, rather than blindly combining all observations. The SSA technical steering group document also notes that existing sensor observation formats lack the needed precision for cis-lunar measurements and communication, which reinforces the need for careful data validation before fusion [N4-F4]. In practice, outlier handling would involve checking observation consistency with orbital constraints, maneuver histories, and sensor geometry, and rejecting observations that do not fit these expectations [N2-F2][N4-F4].

How to prioritize and validate measurements for short-term tracking is closely tied to these quality and consistency requirements. The evidence shows that short-term tracking depends heavily on timely and accurate predicted position information, which in turn depends on reliable tracking data and maneuver information [N2-F2]. The NASA source also explains that good spacecraft design choices and pre-launch coordination can improve identification and tracking, and that position information should be combined with planned maneuver information and sent regularly to conjunction assessment authorities [N2-F2]. This means that for short-term monitoring, the most valuable measurements are those that contribute to the current orbital state and maneuverable behavior, rather than just raw angle-only observations.

The SSA technical steering group document adds another important validation layer: it states that the existing SSA message set is inadequate for cis-lunar tracking and that enhanced message formats are needed to support the maintenance of a new authoritative catalogue [N4-F4]. That suggests that validation should include checking that observations conform to the required message format and precision standards, rather than treating them as interchangeable inputs. In short, the evidence supports a validation workflow where observations are checked for consistency with maneuver information, spacecraft identity, and required message formats, and only validated measurements are used for short-term tracking and conjunction warnings [N2-F2][N4-F4].

Overall, the best practices are: use a broad set of heterogeneous sources, standardize data exchange, assess data quality and consistency, reject or downweight outliers, prioritize measurements that support maneuverable state estimation, and validate against required message and orbit formats [N2-R2][N2-F2][N4-F4].

How to design and operate a cislunar surveillance constellation

The evidence supports a constellation design principle centered on distributed sensing and optimal tasking. The AIAA/ArXiv papers state that constellation design consists of finding the optimally distributed network for performing SSA, while sensor-tasking consists of solving for an optimal tasking strategy [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The same evidence also links sensor-tasking to distributed coordination and complex dynamics in cislunar space [N6-R4]. This indicates that the design should not be a single centralized platform but a network of distributed sensors arranged to maximize coverage and responsiveness, with tasking tailored to the specific dynamics of cislunar motion.

The evidence also suggests that constellation design should be informed by the operational and technical constraints of the cislunar environment. The NASA SSA technical steering group document notes that cis-lunar SSA requires new sensors and a substantially expanded algorithm set, and that current message formats lack the needed precision for cis-lunar observation measurements and communication [N4-F4]. This implies that a cislunar constellation must be designed with both sensing capability and data-processing capability in mind: sensors must be capable of high-precision observations, and the constellation must be able to ingest, process, and disseminate those observations effectively. The same document also emphasizes that the authoritative satellite catalogue must accommodate cis-lunar orbit types, which means that the constellation should be designed to support cataloging and orbit determination across a broader orbital regime [N4-F4].

A key trade-off in constellation design is between sensor density, observation frequency, and operational cost. The evidence points to distributed sensor-tasking methods and optimization approaches that aim to address the complex dynamics of cislunar space and operational cost metrics [N6-R5]. It also notes that low signal-to-noise ratio and lunar exclusion angles are challenges for space-based tracking in cislunar space [N4-R2]. These constraints suggest that increasing sensor density can improve coverage and reduce gaps, but it also increases cost, power, and operational complexity. Conversely, a sparser constellation may be cheaper but may suffer from poor observation frequency and insufficient coverage. The evidence therefore supports a balanced trade-off: optimize the number and placement of sensors so that they can maintain sufficient observation frequency without exceeding cost and operational limits [N6-R5][N4-R2].

The evidence also indicates that constellation architecture should be aligned with short-term monitoring needs. The NASA technical steering group document stresses that an enhanced message set is required to enable cis-lunar SSA, because current formats are not adequate [N4-F4]. This implies that a surveillance constellation should be designed to generate and communicate tracking data in a format that supports short-term monitoring, such as a standardized message set with ephemeris, interpolation, propagation, and covariance fields [N4-F4]. Similarly, the “Cislunar Security National Technical Vision” document describes the technology developments needed to ensure free access, transit, and use of cislunar space, which suggests that the constellation should be designed with operational flexibility and coordination in mind, rather than being a rigid, static architecture [N5-R2]. The constellation should therefore support rapid response, frequent updates, and interoperability with SSA systems and standards.

Another important design principle is the use of sensor-tasking methods that can adapt to cislunar dynamics. The evidence includes a paper on deep reinforcement learning for optimally tasking a narrow-field-of-view ground-based optical telescope for cislunar tracking [N6-R3], as well as a distributed coordinated multi-sensor tasking method for cislunar space [N6-R4]. These examples show that sensor-tasking should not be fixed; instead, it should be dynamic and responsive to the target’s motion, sensor geometry, and observation conditions. The unified orbit-attitude estimation and sensor-tasking framework mentioned in the evidence also shows that tasking can be integrated with state estimation, further supporting a closed-loop design where sensor observations are used to refine tracking and tasking decisions [N7-R5].

Finally, the evidence implies that constellation design should be informed by both performance and cost. The AIAA/ArXiv papers describe optimizing distributed space-based networks from the lens of performance and operational cost metrics [N6-R5]. The NASA technical steering group document similarly notes that the existing SSA message set is not equal to the cis-lunar task and that enhanced messaging is needed [N4-F4]. Together, these sources support a design philosophy in which constellation architecture is optimized not only for coverage and observability but also for cost, interoperability, and long-term maintainability [N6-R5][N4-F4].

In summary, the best design principles are: distributed network architecture, sensor-tasking tailored to cislunar dynamics, high-precision observation capability, standardized message support, and a balance between sensor density, observation frequency, and operational cost [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4][N6-R5][N4-F4]. The constellation should be aligned with short-term monitoring by producing timely, precise, and interoperable tracking data that can support cataloging, conjunction warnings, and rapid response workflows [N4-F4].

What sensing and observation capabilities are needed for cislunar situational awareness

The evidence identifies several sensor types as central to cislunar situational awareness, with optical sensors being especially emphasized. The Air Force Research Laboratory primer states that collected data from sensors are often called observations and that a single image from a telescope with several spacecraft in the field of view can be useful [N1-F1]. The same primer also notes that optical sensors are widely applied to SSA in cislunar space because they can accomplish passive surveillance for nearly the whole cislunar space [N1-F1]. The “Cislunar Security National Technical Vision” document frames the broader sensing problem as requiring new sensors and a substantially expanded algorithm set, reinforcing the need for a sensor portfolio rather than a single sensor type [N5-R2]. The “Motion Hypothesis Satellite Detection for Cislunar Spacecraft” paper further supports that recent work has adapted traditional observing procedures to cislunar ranges, allowing existing ground-based optical systems to be used more effectively [N1-R4]. Together, these sources suggest that optical sensing remains the most effective capability for detecting and tracking cislunar targets, especially because it provides wide-area passive surveillance [N1-F1][N5-R2][N1-R4].

The evidence also shows that optical sensing is not the only important capability, and that radar and lidar are relevant in specific contexts. The NASA primer states that sensor types are a key topic in cislunar observation and that sensor locations matter significantly [N1-F1]. Although the provided evidence does not explicitly describe radar or lidar in cislunar space, the broader SSA literature suggests that these modalities can be useful for complementing optical observations. In particular, the SSA technical steering group document notes that existing sensor observation formats lack the needed precision for cis-lunar measurements [N4-F4], which implies that higher-precision radar or lidar measurements may be needed for certain applications, even if optical sensing remains dominant. The evidence does not provide direct details on radar or lidar performance in cislunar space, so those claims should be treated as plausible but not definitively supported by the provided sources [N1-F1][N4-F4].

The evidence clearly identifies major limitations of optical, radar, lidar, and other sensing modalities in cislunar space. First, cislunar tracking is a novel problem with low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) observations and lunar exclusion angles [N4-R2]. Second, the NASA primer states that cislunar observation is challenging because of sensor locations, and that Earth ground-based, Earth-orbiting, Moon-orbiting, and cislunar space-based sensors each have different constraints [N1-F1]. Third, the “Evaluation Framework for Cislunar Space Domain Awareness” excerpt notes that lunar exclusion angles and solar phase angles both affect SNR drops, meaning that sensor geometry can severely limit visibility [N7-R3]. The “Investigation on Moon-based Sensor Placement for Cislunar Orbit Determination with Exclusion Zones” excerpt similarly states that exclusion zones due to Earth, Sun, and camera field of regard limit the availability of moon-based sensor measurements [N7-R4]. # Integrated approach to comprehensive and accurate cislunar situational awareness

## 1. What this means in practice

Comprehensive and accurate cislunar situational awareness means maintaining a continuous, reliable picture of objects in the cislunar domain so that operators can identify, track, predict, and respond to short-term threats and opportunities. The evidence points to a system in which sensors collect observations, heterogeneous data are fused and validated, orbit determination and prediction algorithms turn those observations into actionable state estimates, and a surveillance constellation is operated to maximize coverage and responsiveness [N8][N9][N10][N11][N12].

In cislunar space, this is especially challenging because the environment is physically and dynamically different from near-Earth space: objects move in non-Keplerian orbits under lunar gravity, signal-to-noise ratios can be low, lunar exclusion angles restrict visibility, and the need for precise message formats and cataloging standards is urgent [N8][N10][N12][N4-F4]. The result is a system that must be distributed, sensor-tasked, and optimized for short-term monitoring, rather than relying on a single centralized architecture or a single sensor type alone [N11][N12].

## 2. Sensor capabilities and observation limits

The most effective sensing capability for cislunar situational awareness is optical sensing. The evidence states that optical sensors are widely applied to SSA in cislunar space because they can accomplish passive surveillance for nearly the whole cislunar space, and that collected data from sensors are often called observations [N1-F1]. The same evidence also notes that recent work has adapted traditional observing procedures to cislunar ranges, allowing existing ground-based optical systems to be used more effectively [N1-R4]. This makes optical sensing the central observation capability, especially for wide-area passive surveillance [N1-F1][N1-R4].

Other sensing modalities are relevant but are not as central in the provided evidence. Radar and lidar may be useful for higher-precision or complementing observations, but the evidence does not provide direct details on their performance in cislunar space [N1-F1]. Instead, the evidence focuses on the limitations of the cislunar environment itself.

### Major limitations

Cislunar tracking is constrained by several physical and operational limits. First, the evidence repeatedly notes low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) observations and lunar exclusion angles [N4-R2][N7-R3]. Second, sensor geometry and lighting conditions matter a great deal: solar phase angles affect SNR drops, and exclusion zones due to Earth, Sun, and camera field of regard limit the availability of moon-based sensor measurements [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Third, long observation ranges across the expansive cislunar domain yield degraded SNR and restrictive observation geometries [N7-R5]. Taken together, these limitations mean that detection probability is highly sensitive to sensor placement, observation timing, and environmental conditions [N4-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4][N7-R5].

### Implication for the integrated approach

Because of these limitations, the integrated approach should not rely on one sensor type alone. Instead, it should use a multi-sensor, distributed sensing architecture optimized for cislunar geometry and lighting. Optical sensors should remain central, but the constellation should also include tasking logic that can select the best sensor at the best time, taking into account exclusion zones and SNR constraints [N1-F1][N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence also supports a broader portfolio of sensors and algorithms, because cislunar SSA requires new sensors and a substantially expanded algorithm set [N5-R2][N4-F4].

## 3. Fusion and processing of heterogeneous data

The evidence shows that SSA data fusion should combine telemetry, tracking, and other data sources into a single coherent picture. The NASA source explains that SSA data is used to predict conjunctions and warn operators of dangerous close approaches, while the Mobility Engineering Technology article states that the system fuses data from satellite telemetry, space weather, orbital proximity, and radio frequency input [N2-F2][N2-R2]. Ansys also defines SSA as the practice of characterizing, tracking, and predicting objects in space around Earth, reinforcing the role of tracking data as a core SSA input [N2-R4].

### Best practices

The best practice is therefore broad-source fusion, not single-source tracking. The evidence supports a multi-source, standardized, and interoperable fusion approach, with telemetry, tracking, and other SSA-relevant inputs combined into a single picture [N2-R2][N2-F2]. Standardized data exchange is also important: the NASA source notes that good spacecraft coordination and standardized data formats such as Orbit Comprehensive Message (OCM) improve identification and tracking [N2-F2]. This means that fusion systems should use standardized message sets and common formats wherever possible.

### Data quality assessment and outlier handling

The evidence also makes clear that raw observations are not enough. The NASA source explains that unidentified objects can remain unidentified for weeks or months, and that misidentification can lead to erroneous warnings being sent to the wrong party [N2-F2]. This implies that the fusion pipeline must include data quality assessment and outlier handling. Observations must be checked against known spacecraft characteristics, maneuver information, and covariance data before they are used for tracking or warning [N2-F2]. The NASA technical steering group document also notes that existing sensor observation formats lack the needed precision for cis-lunar observation measurements, reinforcing the need for careful validation [N4-F4].

### Prioritizing and validating measurements for short-term tracking

For short-term tracking, the most valuable measurements are those that contribute to the current orbital state and maneuverable behavior, rather than just raw angle-only observations. The evidence shows that position information must be combined with planned maneuver information and packaged into a predicted ephemeris, because non-cooperative tracking alone cannot anticipate maneuvers and therefore cannot support robust conjunction assessment [N2-F2]. In short, short-term tracking should prioritize measurements that are consistent with maneuver history, orbital constraints, and expected target behavior [N2-F2][N4-F4].

## 4. Orbit determination and prediction for cislunar targets

The evidence identifies several orbit determination algorithms suitable for non-Earth-orbit objects, especially those that can handle cislunar dynamics. The most cited approach is multi-constrained optimization for initial orbit determination (IOD) using angles-only short-arc observations [N3-F3]. This method integrates measurement, dynamic, and inherent orbital constraints to improve convergence success rate and accuracy [N3-F3]. It is well suited to cislunar space because cislunar orbits are non-Keplerian under lunar gravity and traditional two-body IOD methods are ineffective [N3-F3].

### Suitable algorithms

The evidence also supports a broader family of algorithms: probabilistic target tracking, admissible region-based methods, optimization-based methods, differential corrections, and nonlinear/quasilinear methods [N3-F3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. The physics-informed orbit determination paper states that for chaotic cislunar objects, most orbit determination techniques can only provide state estimates for short periods, which supports the idea that short-term prediction is feasible, but long-term prediction is inherently less reliable [N3-R3]. The non-linear orbit determination methods paper notes that quasilinearization has been presented for orbit determination in general and cis-lunar orbits in particular, and that nonlinear methods are also relevant [N3-R5].

### Short-term prediction accuracy and uncertainty bounds

Short-term prediction accuracy is better than long-term prediction in cislunar space, but uncertainty must still be quantified. The evidence indicates that probabilistic methods can produce an initial state estimate and that uncertainty bounds are part of the output [N3-R4]. The NASA technical steering group document notes that existing sensor observation formats lack the needed precision for cis-lunar measurements, which implies that precise message formats and covariance information are essential for reliable prediction [N4-F4]. The “Evaluation Framework for Cislunar Space Domain Awareness” excerpt also notes that solar phase angles affect SNR drops, which can degrade observation quality and thus the confidence in orbit determination [N7-R3].

### Handling sparse or noisy observations

The evidence shows that sparse or noisy observations are a major challenge in cislunar tracking. The “Cislunar initial orbit determination for angles-only short arcs” paper explicitly addresses short-arc observations and notes that even hours of observation capture only a tiny fraction of the orbit, making cislunar IOD a challenging short-arc problem [N3-F3]. The paper also states that its algorithm was validated across multiple simulation scenarios under a high-fidelity ephemeris model and showed stronger robustness under varying observation geometries [N3-F3]. This suggests that robust optimization, high-fidelity models, and diverse observation geometries are key to handling sparse or noisy observations [N3-F3][N7-R3][N7-R4][N7-R5].

## 5. Constellation design and operation

The evidence supports a distributed sensing and optimal-tasking constellation design. The AIAA/ArXiv papers state that constellation design consists of finding the optimally distributed network for performing SSA, while sensor-tasking consists of solving for an optimal tasking strategy [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The evidence also links sensor-tasking to distributed coordination and complex dynamics in cislunar space [N6-R4]. This means that the surveillance architecture should not be a single centralized platform, but a network of distributed sensors arranged to maximize coverage and responsiveness [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

### Constellation design principles

The key design principles are distributed sensing and optimal tasking. The evidence also emphasizes that constellation design should be informed by the operational and technical constraints of the cislunar environment: new sensors and a substantially expanded algorithm set are needed, and the authoritative satellite catalogue must accommodate cis-lunar orbit types [N5-R2][N4-F4]. The NASA technical steering group document further stresses that an enhanced message set is required to enable cis-lunar SSA, because current formats are inadequate [N4-F4]. This implies that the constellation should be designed to generate and communicate tracking data in a format that supports short-term monitoring, cataloging, and conjunction warnings [N4-F4].

### Trade-offs

The evidence also indicates trade-offs between sensor density, observation frequency, and operational cost. Distributed sensor-tasking methods and optimization approaches aim to address the complex dynamics of cislunar space and operational cost metrics [N6-R5]. At the same time, low SNR and lunar exclusion angles are challenges for space-based tracking [N4-R2]. These constraints suggest that increasing sensor density can improve coverage and reduce gaps, but it also increases cost, power, and operational complexity. Conversely, a sparser constellation may be cheaper but may suffer from poor observation frequency and insufficient coverage. The evidence therefore supports a balanced trade-off: optimize the number and placement of sensors so that they can maintain sufficient observation frequency without exceeding cost and operational limits [N6-R5][N4-R2].

### Alignment with short-term monitoring

The evidence shows that constellation architecture should be aligned with short-term monitoring needs. The upstream constellation-design report argues that the system should be distributed, tasking should be optimal and dynamic, and it should be aligned with short-term monitoring by producing timely, precise, and interoperable tracking data [N11]. This means that the constellation should support rapid re-tasking, frequent updates, and interoperability with SSA systems and standards [N11][N4-F4]. The evidence also supports using sensor-tasking methods such as deep reinforcement learning and distributed coordinated multi-sensor tasking to improve responsiveness [N6-R3][N6-R4].

## 6. Short-term operational workflow and effectiveness criteria

The evidence indicates that short-term tracking and monitoring should prioritize tasks that support rapid identification, conjunction warning, and validated orbit determination. The NASA “Identification and Tracking Systems” source explains that conjunction warnings are essential for collision avoidance, and that position information must be combined with planned maneuver information and packaged into a predicted ephemeris [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that unidentified objects can remain unidentified for weeks or months, and that misidentification can lead to erroneous warnings [N2-F2]. This means that short-term monitoring should prioritize objects that are likely to be maneuverable or have high collision risk, and the workflow should distinguish between high-priority objects and routine observations [N2-F2][N4-F4].

### What to prioritize

The tasks that should be prioritized for short-term tracking are:
- Identification of new or unidentified objects
- Estimation of maneuverable state and planned maneuver information
- Production of validated predicted ephemeris
- Generation of conjunction warnings where needed
- Update of the authoritative satellite catalogue with cis-lunar orbit types [N2-F2][N4-F4]

### How to measure and improve effectiveness

Effectiveness should be measured by response time, data precision, interoperability with message formats, and the ability to support conjunction warnings and cataloging [N4-F4]. The evidence also supports improving effectiveness by using higher-precision observations, better message formats, and more robust algorithms, since the existing SSA message set is not suitable for cis-lunar tracking [N4-F4]. The upstream constellation-design report also provides a useful criterion: effectiveness can be measured by how well the system supports rapid response, frequent observation updates, and dynamic re-tasking [N11].

### Human-in-the-loop considerations and alert/response workflows

The evidence supports a human-in-the-loop workflow because automated systems cannot fully resolve ambiguous identifications. The NASA source explains that conjunction warnings are essential, but also that misidentification can lead to erroneous warnings [N2-F2]. This implies that alerts should be generated only when measurements meet quality thresholds, and responses should be triggered only after human validation or after a threshold of uncertainty is exceeded [N2-F2][N11]. The upstream constellation-design report also suggests that sensor-tasking methods can be optimized dynamically, which supports a workflow in which tasking decisions and alert prioritization are subject to human oversight [N11].

## 7. Integrated approach in one coherent package

### Step 1: Sense with a distributed, multi-sensor constellation

Use a distributed constellation that includes optical and other complementary sensors, optimized for cislunar geometry and lighting conditions. Optical sensors are central for wide-area passive surveillance, but tasking logic should select the best sensor at the best time [N1-F1][N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R4].

### Step 2: Fuse heterogeneous data into a single tracking picture

Combine telemetry, tracking, and other SSA-relevant data sources using standardized, interoperable fusion. Validate observations against maneuver information and covariance data before using them for tracking or warning [N2-F2][N2-R2][N4-F4].

### Step 3: Use robust orbit determination and prediction

Use multi-constrained optimization, probabilistic tracking, admissible region methods, optimization-based methods, differential corrections, and nonlinear/quasilinear methods for orbit determination [N3-F3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. For short-term prediction, rely on the best available state estimate and quantify uncertainty explicitly [N3-R3][N3-R4][N4-F4].

### Step 4: Operate the constellation with optimal sensor-tasking

Design the constellation for distributed sensing and optimal tasking. Use dynamic tasking methods such as deep reinforcement learning and distributed coordinated multi-sensor tasking to improve responsiveness and coverage [N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5].

### Step 5: Align monitoring with short-term operational needs

Prioritize tasks that support rapid identification, conjunction warnings, and validated predicted ephemeris. Measure effectiveness by response time, data precision, interoperability, and ability to support cataloging and warning systems [N4-F4][N11].

### Step 6: Embed human-in-the-loop verification

Use human-in-the-loop verification to resolve ambiguous identifications and trigger alerts only after validated measurements. This ensures that warnings are accurate and that responses are timely [N2-F2][N11].

## 8. Bottom line

Comprehensive and accurate cislunar situational awareness requires a tightly integrated system: sensors, fusion, orbit determination, constellation design, and short-term operational workflow must all work together. The evidence supports an architecture that is distributed, sensor-tasked, and optimized for cislunar dynamics and visibility constraints [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4][N7-R3][N7-R4]. It also supports a workflow in which heterogeneous data are fused, validated, and prioritized to support rapid identification and conjunction warning, while orbit determination and prediction remain the foundation for accurate short-term tracking [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4]. The result is not just better surveillance, but more effective short-term monitoring and response in the challenging cislunar domain [N12].

How to fuse and process heterogeneous data for improved tracking

The evidence points to a clear best practice: SSA data fusion should combine multiple sources into a single coherent picture of space objects, with a special emphasis on telemetry, tracking, and other SSA-relevant inputs. The NASA “Identification and Tracking Systems” source explains that SSA data is used to predict conjunctions and warn operators of dangerous close approaches, which implies that telemetry and tracking data are foundational inputs to the SSA system [N2-F2]. The Mobility Engineering Technology article explicitly states that the system fuses data from satellite telemetry, space weather, orbital proximity, and radio frequency input [N2-R2]. Ansys’s definition of SSA as the practice of characterizing, tracking, and predicting objects in space around Earth also supports the idea that tracking data are part of the core SSA workflow [N2-R4].

Best practices for fusing telemetry, tracking, and other data sources therefore include using a broad set of inputs, not relying on a single sensor type, and ensuring that the resulting data can support conjunction assessment and collision avoidance. The NASA source also highlights that good spacecraft coordination and standardized data formats such as Orbit Comprehensive Message (OCM) improve identification and tracking, which means that interoperability and standardized telemetry exchange are important fusion best practices [N2-F2]. In short, the evidence supports a multi-source, standardized, and interoperable fusion approach rather than a single-sensor-only strategy [N2-R2][N2-F2].

The role of data quality assessment and outlier handling is also implied by the evidence. The NASA source stresses that identification and tracking are difficult when objects are deployed closely together, leading to “CubeSat confusion” and a large number of possible identification combinations [N2-F2]. This suggests that raw observations are not enough: they need validation against known spacecraft characteristics, maneuver information, and covariance data. The same source also emphasizes that position information must be combined with planned maneuver information and packaged into a predicted ephemeris, because non-cooperative tracking alone cannot anticipate maneuvers and therefore cannot support robust conjunction assessment [N2-F2]. This is a key quality-assessment step: any measurement should be checked against expected maneuver behavior, and outliers or inconsistent observations should be flagged or excluded before they affect the ephemeris.

For outlier handling, the evidence indirectly supports rejection or downweighting of inconsistent or low-quality observations. The NASA source says that unidentified objects can remain unidentified for weeks or months, and that misidentification can lead to erroneous warnings being sent to the wrong party [N2-F2]. That implies that the fusion pipeline should include mechanisms to detect and resolve ambiguous associations, rather than blindly combining all observations. The SSA technical steering group document also notes that existing sensor observation formats lack the needed precision for cis-lunar measurements and communication, which reinforces the need for careful data validation before fusion [N4-F4]. In practice, outlier handling would involve checking observation consistency with orbital constraints, maneuver histories, and sensor geometry, and rejecting observations that do not fit these expectations [N2-F2][N4-F4].

How to prioritize and validate measurements for short-term tracking is closely tied to these quality and consistency requirements. The SSA technical steering group document adds another important validation layer: it states that the existing SSA message set is inadequate for cis-lunar tracking and that enhanced message formats are needed to support the maintenance of a new authoritative catalogue [N4-F4]. Overall, the best practices are: use a broad set of heterogeneous sources, standardize data exchange, assess data quality and consistency, reject or downweight outliers, prioritize measurements that support maneuverable state estimation, and validate against required message and orbit formats [N2-R2][N2-F2][N4-F4].

# Integrated approach to comprehensive and accurate cislunar situational awareness

## 1. What this means in practice

Comprehensive and accurate cislunar situational awareness means maintaining a continuous, reliable picture of objects in the cislunar domain so that operators can identify, track, predict, and respond to short-term threats and opportunities. The evidence points to a system in which sensors collect observations, heterogeneous data are fused and validated, orbit determination and prediction algorithms turn those observations into actionable state estimates, and a surveillance constellation is operated to maximize coverage and responsiveness [N8][N9][N10][N11][N12].

In cislunar space, this is especially challenging because the environment is physically and dynamically different from near-Earth space: objects move in non-Keplerian orbits under lunar gravity, signal-to-noise ratios can be low, lunar exclusion angles restrict visibility, and the need for precise message formats and cataloging standards is urgent [N8][N10][N12][N4-F4]. The result is a system that must be distributed, sensor-tasked, and optimized for short-term monitoring, rather than relying on a single centralized architecture or a single sensor type alone [N11][N12].

## 2. Sensor capabilities and observation limits

The most effective sensing capability for cislunar situational awareness is optical sensing. The evidence states that optical sensors are widely applied to SSA in cislunar space because they can accomplish passive surveillance for nearly the whole cislunar space, and that collected data from sensors are often called observations [N1-F1]. The same evidence also notes that recent work has adapted traditional observing procedures to cislunar ranges, allowing existing ground-based optical systems to be used more effectively [N1-R4]. This makes optical sensing the central observation capability, especially for wide-area passive surveillance [N1-F1][N1-R4].

Other sensing modalities are relevant but are not as central in the provided evidence. Radar and lidar may be useful for higher-precision or complementing observations, but the evidence does not provide direct details on their performance in cislunar space [N1-F1]. Instead, the evidence focuses on the limitations of the cislunar environment itself.

### Major limitations

Cislunar tracking is constrained by several physical and operational limits. First, the evidence repeatedly notes low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) observations and lunar exclusion angles [N4-R2][N7-R3]. Second, sensor geometry and lighting conditions matter a great deal: solar phase angles affect SNR drops, and exclusion zones due to Earth, Sun, and camera field of regard limit the availability of moon-based sensor measurements [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Third, long observation ranges across the expansive cislunar domain yield degraded SNR and restrictive observation geometries [N7-R5]. Taken together, these limitations mean that detection probability is highly sensitive to sensor placement, observation timing, and environmental conditions [N4-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4][N7-R5].

### Implication for the integrated approach

Because of these limitations, the integrated approach should not rely on one sensor type alone. Instead, it should use a multi-sensor, distributed sensing architecture optimized for cislunar geometry and lighting. Optical sensors should remain central, but the constellation should also include tasking logic that can select the best sensor at the best time, taking into account exclusion zones and SNR constraints [N1-F1][N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence also supports a broader portfolio of sensors and algorithms, because cislunar SSA requires new sensors and a substantially expanded algorithm set [N5-R2][N4-F4].

## 3. Fusion and processing of heterogeneous data

The evidence shows that SSA data fusion should combine telemetry, tracking, and other data sources into a single coherent picture. The NASA source explains that SSA data is used to predict conjunctions and warn operators of dangerous close approaches, while the Mobility Engineering Technology article states that the system fuses data from satellite telemetry, space weather, orbital proximity, and radio frequency input [N2-F2][N2-R2]. Ansys also defines SSA as the practice of characterizing, tracking, and predicting objects in space around Earth, reinforcing the role of tracking data as a core SSA input [N2-R4].

### Best practices

The best practice is therefore broad-source fusion, not single-source tracking. The evidence supports a multi-source, standardized, and interoperable fusion approach, with telemetry, tracking, and other SSA-relevant inputs combined into a single picture [N2-R2][N2-F2]. Standardized data exchange is also important: the NASA source notes that good spacecraft coordination and standardized data formats such as Orbit Comprehensive Message (OCM) improve identification and tracking [N2-F2]. This means that fusion systems should use standardized message sets and common formats wherever possible.

### Data quality assessment and outlier handling

The evidence also makes clear that raw observations are not enough. The NASA source explains that unidentified objects can remain unidentified for weeks or months, and that misidentification can lead to erroneous warnings being sent to the wrong party [N2-F2]. This implies that the fusion pipeline must include data quality assessment and outlier handling. Observations must be checked against known spacecraft characteristics, maneuver information, and covariance data before they are used for tracking or warning [N2-F2]. The NASA technical steering group document also notes that existing sensor observation formats lack the needed precision for cis-lunar observation measurements, reinforcing the need for careful validation [N4-F4].

### Prioritizing and validating measurements for short-term tracking

For short-term tracking, the most valuable measurements are those that contribute to the current orbital state and maneuverable behavior, rather than just raw angle-only observations. The evidence shows that position information must be combined with planned maneuver information and packaged into a predicted ephemeris, because non-cooperative tracking alone cannot anticipate maneuvers and therefore cannot support robust conjunction assessment [N2-F2]. In short, short-term tracking should prioritize measurements that are consistent with maneuver history, orbital constraints, and expected target behavior [N2-F2][N4-F4].

## 4. Orbit determination and prediction for cislunar targets

The evidence identifies several orbit determination algorithms suitable for non-Earth-orbit objects, especially those that can handle cislunar dynamics. The most cited approach is multi-constrained optimization for initial orbit determination (IOD) using angles-only short-arc observations [N3-F3]. This method integrates measurement, dynamic, and inherent orbital constraints to improve convergence success rate and accuracy [N3-F3]. It is well suited to cislunar space because cislunar orbits are non-Keplerian under lunar gravity and traditional two-body IOD methods are ineffective [N3-F3].

### Suitable algorithms

The evidence also supports a broader family of algorithms: probabilistic target tracking, admissible region-based methods, optimization-based methods, differential corrections, and nonlinear/quasilinear methods [N3-F3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. The physics-informed orbit determination paper states that for chaotic cislunar objects, most orbit determination techniques can only provide state estimates for short periods, which supports the idea that short-term prediction is feasible, but long-term prediction is inherently less reliable [N3-R3]. The non-linear orbit determination methods paper notes that quasilinearization has been presented for orbit determination in general and cis-lunar orbits in particular, and that nonlinear methods are also relevant [N3-R5].

### Short-term prediction accuracy and uncertainty bounds

Short-term prediction accuracy is better than long-term prediction in cislunar space, but uncertainty must still be quantified. The evidence indicates that probabilistic methods can produce an initial state estimate and that uncertainty bounds are part of the output [N3-R4]. The NASA technical steering group document notes that existing sensor observation formats lack the needed precision for cis-lunar measurements, which implies that precise message formats and covariance information are essential for reliable prediction [N4-F4]. The “Evaluation Framework for Cislunar Space Domain Awareness” excerpt also notes that solar phase angles affect SNR drops, which can degrade observation quality and thus the confidence in orbit determination [N7-R3].

### Handling sparse or noisy observations

The evidence shows that sparse or noisy observations are a major challenge in cislunar tracking. The “Cislunar initial orbit determination for angles-only short arcs” paper explicitly addresses short-arc observations and notes that even hours of observation capture only a tiny fraction of the orbit, making cislunar IOD a challenging short-arc problem [N3-F3]. The paper also states that its algorithm was validated across multiple simulation scenarios under a high-fidelity ephemeris model and showed stronger robustness under varying observation geometries [N3-F3]. This suggests that robust optimization, high-fidelity models, and diverse observation geometries are key to handling sparse or noisy observations [N3-F3][N7-R3][N7-R4][N7-R5].

## 5. Constellation design and operation

The evidence supports a distributed sensing and optimal-tasking constellation design. The AIAA/ArXiv papers state that constellation design consists of finding the optimally distributed network for performing SSA, while sensor-tasking consists of solving for an optimal tasking strategy [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The evidence also links sensor-tasking to distributed coordination and complex dynamics in cislunar space [N6-R4]. This means that the surveillance architecture should not be a single centralized platform, but a network of distributed sensors arranged to maximize coverage and responsiveness [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

### Constellation design principles

The key design principles are distributed sensing and optimal tasking. The evidence also emphasizes that constellation design should be informed by the operational and technical constraints of the cislunar environment: new sensors and a substantially expanded algorithm set are needed, and the authoritative satellite catalogue must accommodate cis-lunar orbit types [N5-R2][N4-F4]. The NASA technical steering group document further stresses that an enhanced message set is required to enable cis-lunar SSA, because current formats are inadequate [N4-F4]. This implies that the constellation should be designed to generate and communicate tracking data in a format that supports short-term monitoring, cataloging, and conjunction warnings [N4-F4].

### Trade-offs

The evidence also indicates trade-offs between sensor density, observation frequency, and operational cost. Distributed sensor-tasking methods and optimization approaches aim to address the complex dynamics of cislunar space and operational cost metrics [N6-R5]. At the same time, low SNR and lunar exclusion angles are challenges for space-based tracking [N4-R2]. These constraints suggest that increasing sensor density can improve coverage and reduce gaps, but it also increases cost, power, and operational complexity. Conversely, a sparser constellation may be cheaper but may suffer from poor observation frequency and insufficient coverage. The evidence therefore supports a balanced trade-off: optimize the number and placement of sensors so that they can maintain sufficient observation frequency without exceeding cost and operational limits [N6-R5][N4-R2].

### Alignment with short-term monitoring

The evidence shows that constellation architecture should be aligned with short-term monitoring needs. The upstream constellation-design report argues that the system should be distributed, tasking should be optimal and dynamic, and it should be aligned with short-term monitoring by producing timely, precise, and interoperable tracking data [N11]. This means that the constellation should support rapid re-tasking, frequent updates, and interoperability with SSA systems and standards [N11][N4-F4]. The evidence also supports using sensor-tasking methods such as deep reinforcement learning and distributed coordinated multi-sensor tasking to improve responsiveness [N6-R3][N6-R4].

## 6. Short-term operational workflow and effectiveness criteria

The evidence indicates that short-term tracking and monitoring should prioritize tasks that support rapid identification, conjunction warning, and validated orbit determination. The NASA “Identification and Tracking Systems” source explains that conjunction warnings are essential for collision avoidance, and that position information must be combined with planned maneuver information and packaged into a predicted ephemeris [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that unidentified objects can remain unidentified for weeks or months, and that misidentification can lead to erroneous warnings [N2-F2]. This means that short-term monitoring should prioritize objects that are likely to be maneuverable or have high collision risk, and the workflow should distinguish between high-priority objects and routine observations [N2-F2][N4-F4].

### What to prioritize

The tasks that should be prioritized for short-term tracking are:
- Identification of new or unidentified objects
- Estimation of maneuverable state and planned maneuver information
- Production of validated predicted ephemeris
- Generation of conjunction warnings where needed
- Update of the authoritative satellite catalogue with cis-lunar orbit types [N2-F2][N4-F4]

### How to measure and improve effectiveness

Effectiveness should be measured by response time, data precision, interoperability with message formats, and the ability to support conjunction warnings and cataloging [N4-F4]. The evidence also supports improving effectiveness by using higher-precision observations, better message formats, and more robust algorithms, since the existing SSA message set is not suitable for cis-lunar tracking [N4-F4]. The upstream constellation-design report also provides a useful criterion: effectiveness can be measured by how well the system supports rapid response, frequent observation updates, and dynamic re-tasking [N11].

### Human-in-the-loop considerations and alert/response workflows

The evidence supports a human-in-the-loop workflow because automated systems cannot fully resolve ambiguous identifications. The NASA source explains that conjunction warnings are essential, but also that misidentification can lead to erroneous warnings [N2-F2]. This implies that alerts should be generated only when measurements meet quality thresholds, and responses should be triggered only after human validation or after a threshold of uncertainty is exceeded [N2-F2][N11]. The upstream constellation-design report also suggests that sensor-tasking methods can be optimized dynamically, which supports a workflow in which tasking decisions and alert prioritization are subject to human oversight [N11].

## 7. Integrated approach in one coherent package

### Step 1: Sense with a distributed, multi-sensor constellation

Use a distributed constellation that includes optical and other complementary sensors, optimized for cislunar geometry and lighting conditions. Optical sensors are central for wide-area passive surveillance, but tasking logic should select the best sensor at the best time [N1-F1][N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R4].

### Step 2: Fuse heterogeneous data into a single tracking picture

Combine telemetry, tracking, and other SSA-relevant data sources using standardized, interoperable fusion. Validate observations against maneuver information and covariance data before using them for tracking or warning [N2-F2][N2-R2][N4-F4].

### Step 3: Use robust orbit determination and prediction

Use multi-constrained optimization, probabilistic tracking, admissible region methods, optimization-based methods, differential corrections, and nonlinear/quasilinear methods for orbit determination [N3-F3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. For short-term prediction, rely on the best available state estimate and quantify uncertainty explicitly [N3-R3][N3-R4][N4-F4].

### Step 4: Operate the constellation with optimal sensor-tasking

Design the constellation for distributed sensing and optimal tasking. Use dynamic tasking methods such as deep reinforcement learning and distributed coordinated multi-sensor tasking to improve responsiveness and coverage [N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5].

### Step 5: Align monitoring with short-term operational needs

Prioritize tasks that support rapid identification, conjunction warnings, and validated predicted ephemeris. Measure effectiveness by response time, data precision, interoperability, and ability to support cataloging and warning systems [N4-F4][N11].

### Step 6: Embed human-in-the-loop verification

Use human-in-the-loop verification to resolve ambiguous identifications and trigger alerts only after validated measurements. This ensures that warnings are accurate and that responses are timely [N2-F2][N11].

## 8. Bottom line

Comprehensive and accurate cislunar situational awareness requires a tightly integrated system: sensors, fusion, orbit determination, constellation design, and short-term operational workflow must all work together. The evidence supports an architecture that is distributed, sensor-tasked, and optimized for cislunar dynamics and visibility constraints [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4][N7-R3][N7-R4]. It also supports a workflow in which heterogeneous data are fused, validated, and prioritized to support rapid identification and conjunction warning, while orbit determination and prediction remain the foundation for accurate short-term tracking [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4]. The result is not just better surveillance, but more effective short-term monitoring and response in the challenging cislunar domain [N12].

How to fuse and process heterogeneous data for improved tracking

The evidence points to a clear best practice: SSA data fusion should combine multiple sources into a single coherent picture of space objects, with a special emphasis on telemetry, tracking, and other SSA-relevant inputs. The NASA “Identification and Tracking Systems” source explains that SSA data is used to predict conjunctions and warn operators of dangerous close approaches, which implies that telemetry and tracking data are foundational inputs to the SSA system [N2-F2]. The Mobility Engineering Technology article explicitly states that the system fuses data from satellite telemetry, space weather, orbital proximity, and radio frequency input [N2-R2]. Ansys’s definition of SSA as the practice of characterizing, tracking, and predicting objects in space around Earth also supports the idea that tracking data are part of the core SSA workflow [N2-R4].

Best practices for fusing telemetry, tracking, and other data sources therefore include using a broad set of inputs, not relying on a single sensor type, and ensuring that the resulting data can support conjunction assessment and collision avoidance. The NASA source also highlights that good spacecraft coordination and standardized data formats such as Orbit Comprehensive Message (OCM) improve identification and tracking, which means that interoperability and standardized telemetry exchange are important fusion best practices [N2-F2]. In short, the evidence supports a multi-source, standardized, and interoperable fusion approach rather than a single-sensor-only strategy [N2-R2][N2-F2].

The role of data quality assessment and outlier handling is also implied by the evidence. The NASA source stresses that identification and tracking are difficult when objects are deployed closely together, leading to “CubeSat confusion” and a large number of possible identification combinations [N2-F2]. This suggests that raw observations are not enough: they need validation against known spacecraft characteristics, maneuver information, and covariance data. The same source also emphasizes that position information must be combined with planned maneuver information and packaged into a predicted ephemeris, because non-cooperative tracking alone cannot anticipate maneuvers and therefore cannot support robust conjunction assessment [N2-F2]. This is a key quality-assessment step: any measurement should be checked against expected maneuver behavior, and outliers or inconsistent observations should be flagged or excluded before they affect the ephemeris.

For outlier handling, the evidence indirectly supports rejection or downweighting of inconsistent or low-quality observations. The NASA source says that unidentified objects can remain unidentified for weeks or months, and that misidentification can lead to erroneous warnings being sent to the wrong party [N2-F2]. That implies that the fusion pipeline should include mechanisms to detect and resolve ambiguous associations, rather than blindly combining all observations. The SSA technical steering group document also notes that existing sensor observation formats lack the needed precision for cis-lunar measurements and communication, which reinforces the need for careful data validation before fusion [N4-F4]. In practice, outlier handling would involve checking observation consistency with orbital constraints, maneuver histories, and sensor geometry, and rejecting observations that do not fit these expectations [N2-F2][N4-F4].

How to prioritize and validate measurements for short-term tracking is closely tied to these quality and consistency requirements. The evidence shows that short-term tracking depends heavily on timely and accurate predicted position information, which in turn depends on reliable tracking data and maneuver information [N2-F2]. The NASA source also explains that good spacecraft design choices and pre-launch coordination can improve identification and tracking, and that position information should be combined with planned maneuver information and sent regularly to conjunction assessment authorities [N2-F2]. This means that for short-term monitoring, the most valuable measurements are those that contribute to the current orbital state and maneuverable behavior, rather than just raw angle-only observations.

The SSA technical steering group document adds another important validation layer: it states that the existing SSA message set is inadequate for cis-lunar tracking and that enhanced message formats are needed to support the maintenance of a new authoritative catalogue [N4-F4]. That suggests that validation should include checking that observations conform to the required message format and precision standards, rather than treating them as interchangeable inputs. In short, the evidence supports a validation workflow where observations are checked for consistency with maneuver information, spacecraft identity, and required message formats, and only validated measurements are used for short-term tracking and conjunction warnings [N2-F2][N4-F4].

Overall, the best practices are: use a broad set of heterogeneous sources, standardize data exchange, assess data quality and consistency, reject or downweight outliers, prioritize measurements that support maneuverable state estimation, and validate against required message and orbit formats [N2-R2][N2-F2][N4-F4].

The evidence supports a constellation design principle centered on distributed sensing and optimal tasking. The evidence also suggests that constellation design should be informed by the operational and technical constraints of the cislunar environment. The NASA SSA technical steering group document notes that cis-lunar SSA requires new sensors and a substantially expanded algorithm set, and that current message formats lack the needed precision for cis-lunar observation measurements and communication [N4-F4]. The same document also emphasizes that the authoritative satellite catalogue must accommodate cis-lunar orbit types, which means that the constellation should be designed to support cataloging and orbit determination across a broader orbital regime [N4-F4].

A key trade-off in constellation design is between sensor density, observation frequency, and operational cost. The evidence points to distributed sensor-tasking methods and optimization approaches that aim to address the complex dynamics of cislunar space and operational cost metrics [N6-R5]. It also notes that low signal-to-noise ratio and lunar exclusion angles are challenges for space-based tracking in cislunar space [N4-R2]. These constraints suggest that increasing sensor density can improve coverage and reduce gaps, but it also increases cost, power, and operational complexity. Conversely, a sparser constellation may be cheaper but may suffer from poor observation frequency and insufficient coverage. The evidence therefore supports a balanced trade-off: optimize the number and placement of sensors so that they can maintain sufficient observation frequency without exceeding cost and operational limits [N6-R5][N4-R2].

The evidence also indicates that constellation architecture should be aligned with short-term monitoring needs. The NASA technical steering group document stresses that an enhanced message set is required to enable cis-lunar SSA, because current formats are not adequate [N4-F4]. This implies that a surveillance constellation should be designed to generate and communicate tracking data in a format that supports short-term monitoring, such as a standardized message set with ephemeris, interpolation, propagation, and covariance fields [N4-F4]. Similarly, the “Cislunar Security National Technical Vision” document describes the technology developments needed to ensure free access, transit, and use of cislunar space, which suggests that the constellation should be designed with operational flexibility and coordination in mind, rather than being a rigid, static architecture [N5-R2]. Finally, the evidence implies that constellation design should be informed by both performance and cost. The AIAA/ArXiv papers describe optimizing distributed space-based networks from the lens of performance and operational cost metrics [N6-R5]. The NASA technical steering group document similarly notes that the existing SSA message set is not equal to the cis-lunar task and that enhanced messaging is needed [N4-F4]. Together, these sources support a design philosophy in which constellation architecture is optimized not only for coverage and observability but also for cost, interoperability, and long-term maintainability [N6-R5][N4-F4].

In summary, the best design principles are: distributed network architecture, sensor-tasking tailored to cislunar dynamics, high-precision observation capability, standardized message support, and a balance between sensor density, observation frequency, and operational cost [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4][N6-R5][N4-F4]. The evidence clearly identifies major limitations of optical, radar, lidar, and other sensing modalities in cislunar space.
